questions.q: In this lesson's framing, what does it mean to say a matrix M represents a 'linear transformation'?
options: M is a transformation only in the sense that it changes shape when printed on a page
M defines a consistent rule that maps any input vector v to an output vector Mv, via matrix-vector multiplication
M is a linear transformation only if all of its entries are equal to 1
M only works on one specific vector and cannot be applied to any other
questions.explain: A linear transformation is the geometric meaning behind matrix-vector multiplication: feed the matrix any vector and it applies the same fixed rule, producing a new vector.

questions.q: Using the 90-degree rotation matrix R_90 = [[0,-1],[1,0]], what is R_90 applied to v = (1,0)?
questions.explain: R_90 * (1,0) = ((0)(1)+(-1)(0), (1)(1)+(0)(0)) = (0,1) -- the vector pointing right rotates to point straight up, a 90-degree counterclockwise turn.

questions.q: What does multiplying the Pauli-X matrix [[0,1],[1,0]] by the vector |0> = (1,0) produce, and what does this represent physically?
options: (1,0), meaning X leaves every qubit state unchanged
(0,1), which equals |1> -- X flips the qubit state, acting as the quantum bit-flip (NOT) gate
(0,0), meaning X erases the qubit state entirely
(1,1), meaning X puts the qubit into an equal superposition
questions.explain: X|0> = ((0)(1)+(1)(0), (1)(1)+(0)(0)) = (0,1) = |1>, confirming X is the bit-flip gate: it turns |0> into |1> (and, symmetrically, |1> into |0>).

questions.q: The lesson applies R_90 to both v = (1,0) and w = (2,1), getting different output vectors each time. Why does this NOT contradict the claim that R_90 is a single, consistent linear transformation?
options: Because a linear transformation applies the same fixed rule to every input, and different inputs are expected to produce different outputs -- consistency means the RULE doesn't change, not that the OUTPUT is identical for every vector
Because R_90 secretly changes its own entries between the two multiplications
It does contradict the claim, since a true linear transformation must always output the same vector regardless of input
Because only one of the two multiplications was performed correctly
questions.explain: A linear transformation is one fixed rule (the matrix) consistently applied; naturally, different input vectors generally produce different output vectors under that same rule.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the relationship between 'applying a quantum gate' and 'matrix-vector multiplication'?
options: Matrix-vector multiplication only approximates what a gate does, it isn't exact
Gates act on qubits without ever being represented as matrices
They are the same operation -- a gate's entire effect on a qubit state is computed by multiplying the gate's matrix by the state's vector, with no additional special quantum arithmetic
Applying a gate requires a separate kind of arithmetic that only works on quantum computers
questions.explain: The lesson's central point is that a gate's action on a state is exactly ordinary matrix-vector multiplication, as shown with X|0> and X|1> using the same row-times-column arithmetic from Lesson 6.
